dialogs.title: Dialogue — Flyttdagen
dialogs.intro: After a year in the student corridor at Lappis, Dian is moving into a shared flat — a *kollektiv* — on Södermalm with Elin and Elin's younger brother Jonas. The hallway is already full of boxes.

notes: **När jag flyttade hit kände jag ingen** — the whole time clause stands in first place, so the main verb (*kände*) comes straight after it and the subject (*jag*) follows. Read it as one block + verb: [*När jag flyttade hit*] **kände** *jag*… English just adds a comma; Swedish swaps the order. This is the single most common word-order slip at A2.

**Innan** (before) introduces a clause: *innan jag somnar*. Before a plain noun, written Swedish prefers **före**: *före middagen*, *före jul*. In speech you'll hear *innan* in both places, so don't worry if Swedes break this rule.

**Efter att vi har ätit** — before a clause, "after" is **efter att**; before a noun it's just **efter**: *efter maten*. In relaxed speech many Swedes drop the *att* (*efter vi har ätit*), but keep it in writing.

**Sedan jag vaknade** — *sedan* (often said **sen**) has a new job here: "since", introducing a clause. You already know it as "then" (*Sedan vilade jag*) and from *för … sedan* ("ago"). The main verb is usually in the perfect, just as in English: *Jag **har burit** lådor sedan jag vaknade.*

**I hallen så länge** — *så länge* here means "for now, for the time being", not "as long as". A **kollektiv** (**kol-lek-TEEV**) is a shared flat or house; with Stockholm's famously long housing queue (*bostadskön*), it's how many young people live.

**Det känns redan som hemma** — *det känns* means "it feels": *Hur känns det?* (How does it feel?). And **fika** is a verb as well as a noun: *Vi har fikat ihop* — we've had coffee and something sweet together. A Swedish friendship often starts exactly there.

grammars.title: Time clauses
body: These words all start a subordinate clause that says **when** something happens in relation to something else. The clause can come after the main clause or in front of it.

head: Conjunction
Meaning
Example
rows: **När** jag flyttade hit kände jag ingen.
Jag måste packa upp **innan** jag somnar.
**Efter att** vi har ätit tar vi en promenad.
Jag har burit lådor **sedan** jag vaknade.
Vi stannar ute **tills** det blir mörkt.
Ring mig **så fort** du är framme.
Vi säger ingenting **förrän** vi har fikat.

after: **När** covers "when" for a single event in the past, for repeated events and for the future. (German learners: there's no separate *als*.) It is also the question word: *När kommer du?*
As in English, there's no future form inside a time clause: *innan jag somnar* (before I fall asleep), never *innan jag ska somna*.
Time clause first → main verb next → subject after: *Så fort jag kom hem **ringde** jag mamma.*

grammars.title: BIFF inside time clauses
body: Every time clause is a subordinate clause, so the BIFF rule from Swedish 101 applies: *inte* — and the other sentence adverbs like *aldrig, alltid, redan, ofta* — jump in front of the finite verb.
after: With two verbs, the adverb goes before the **first** one: *när jag **inte har** druckit kaffe*, not *när jag har inte druckit*.
The main clause that follows still has its own rules: *När jag inte har druckit kaffe **kan** jag **inte** tänka.* Subordinate clause: *inte* before the verb. Main clause: *inte* after it.

grammars.title: Sedan: three jobs

head: Job
Word order
Example
rows: Jag har bott här **sedan** jag kom.

after: In speech all three are usually **sen**. Context sorts them out, just as it does for English "since" (time) and "since" (because).

blocks.text: Most Swedish apartment buildings have a **tvättstuga** in the basement: a shared laundry room that you book in advance, often with a little lock or a magnetic tag on a board. Leaving your clothes in the machine after your slot ends is a famous source of neighbor drama — and of passive-aggressive notes taped to the wall.

blocks.title: House rules in a kollektiv
items: *Vi delar på hyran och maten.* — We split the rent and the food.
*Den som lagar mat diskar inte.* — Whoever cooks doesn't do the dishes.
*Städschemat sitter på kylskåpet.* — The cleaning rota is on the fridge.
*Säg till innan du bjuder hem folk.* — Tell us before you invite people over.

sections.title: Putting two events on one timeline

blocks.text: The words in this unit let you tell a story with depth instead of a flat list. Compare a beginner's version — *Jag flyttade hit. Jag kände ingen. Jag lärde mig svenska.* — with an A2 version: *När jag flyttade hit kände jag ingen, men sedan jag började läsa svenska har jag fått många vänner.*

items: **at the same time:** *medan* — *Medan Jonas övar läser Elin.*
**one after the other:** *innan, efter att, så fort* — *Så fort jag kom hem somnade jag.*
**up to a point:** *tills, inte … förrän* — *Vi väntade tills bussen kom.*
**from a point up to now:** *sedan* + perfect — *Jag har bott på Söder sedan i augusti.*

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Swedish 101, Unit 18
items: Say five subordinate clauses with *inte* in them, using *eftersom, att, om, när, som*.
Then turn each one around so that it stands first: *Eftersom jag inte förstår, frågar jag* — and check that the main verb comes right after the comma.
